allObjections.title: Backup verification insufficient for data loss
allObjections.detail: §3.3 S3 5th pillar requires pg_dump backup but only verifies via checksum and row counts. A corrupted backup that passes checksum but has subtle data corruption in column values would not be detected until after irreversible DROP COLUMN executes.

allObjections.title: SSRF probe set incomplete
allObjections.detail: §3.4 S4 7th pillar SSRF probes omit critical vectors: SSRF via redirect chains, protocol smuggling (gopher://), and cloud-specific IMDSv2 token bypass techniques. The probe set tests only basic direct-request patterns.

allObjections.title: Rate limit default too permissive
allObjections.detail: §3.4 S4 8th pillar defaults to 60 req/min for undeclared endpoints. For mutation endpoints or resource-intensive operations, this default allows significant abuse potential before triggering 429 responses.

allObjections.title: Schema migration lock timeout missing
allObjections.detail: §3.3 S3 3rd pillar requires <5s completion under p99 load but specifies no lock acquisition timeout. A migration could wait indefinitely for locks, causing production outages without automatic abort.

allObjections.title: Data-loss prevention complexity
allObjections.detail: The addition of the 5th pillar in §3.3 for data-loss prevention introduces significant complexity. It requires explicit rationale citation, verified backups, and admin roles, which could slow down the development process and increase the risk of human error in managing these requirements.

allObjections.title: Non-overridable security suite
allObjections.detail: The §3.4 security suite is non-overridable, which could lead to bottlenecks in development if false positives occur. The inability to bypass these checks, even temporarily, could delay critical updates or fixes.

allObjections.title: Scope of construction classes
allObjections.detail: The construction classes in §2 impose strict limits on file and line counts, which may not be sufficient for more complex operations. This could lead to incomplete implementations or the need for multiple operations to achieve a single goal, increasing overhead.

allObjections.title: Insufficient Rollback
allObjections.detail: The proposal does not provide a clear rollback strategy in case of failures during the construction process, which could lead to system instability. Specifically, §3.3 S3 — Schema migration testing does not outline a comprehensive rollback plan.

allObjections.title: Overly Complex Security Suite
allObjections.detail: The 8-pillar security-test suite in §3.4 S4 — Construction security suite may be overly complex and difficult to maintain, potentially leading to false negatives or positives. The addition of new pillars such as SSRF and rate-limit probes may increase the complexity of the suite.

allObjections.title: Inadequate Operator Role Definition
allObjections.detail: The proposal does not provide a clear definition of the operator role and its responsibilities, which could lead to confusion and errors during the construction process. Specifically, the requirement for an admin role in §3.3 S3 — Schema migration testing is not clearly defined.

allObjections.title: Schema migration complexity
allObjections.detail: The proposed 5th pillar in §3.3 S3 introduces significant complexity. The requirement for a pre-migration backup and its verification adds additional steps that could delay the migration process and increase the risk of human error.

allObjections.title: Overly restrictive security suite
allObjections.detail: The extension of S4 to include SSRF and rate-limit probes, along with the non-overridable nature of these checks, may lead to false positives and unnecessary blockages. This could hinder the development process and delay the deployment of critical features.

allObjections.title: Lack of rollback path
allObjections.detail: The proposal does not specify a clear rollback path for schema migrations that fail the data-loss prevention checks. This could lead to incomplete or failed migrations that are difficult to recover from, impacting system stability and data integrity.

allObjections.title: Complexity increase
allObjections.detail: Adding a 5th pillar to S3 and extending S4 to 8 pillars significantly increases the complexity of the construction process, potentially leading to longer development cycles and higher maintenance costs.

allObjections.title: False positives risk
allObjections.detail: The new data-loss prevention (DLP) pillar in S3 may generate false positives, blocking legitimate destructive migrations and causing unnecessary delays in the construction process.

allObjections.title: Over-engineering concern
allObjections.detail: The proposal to strengthen S4 further by adding CSRF and prototype-pollution probes may be considered over-engineering, as these issues might be better addressed through other means, such as code reviews or runtime protections.

allObjections.title: §3.3 S3: Backup verification weakness
allObjections.detail: The backup verification in S3 only checks row counts and checksums. It doesn't verify data integrity or consistency, potentially missing subtle data corruption issues introduced during the backup/restore process. A malicious actor could manipulate data in a way that doesn't affect row counts or checksums but still compromises the system.

allObjections.title: §3.4 S4: SSRF probe limitations
allObjections.detail: The SSRF probes in S4 use a predefined set of payloads. This approach is vulnerable to bypasses if the application uses custom URL parsing or filtering logic. Attackers can craft SSRF payloads that are not detected by the standard probes but still allow them to access internal resources.

allObjections.title: §3.4 S4: Rate-limit default value
allObjections.detail: The rate-limit pillar defaults to 60 req/min if undeclared. This default might be too high for some endpoints, especially those that perform resource-intensive operations. A lower default or a mechanism to dynamically adjust the rate limit based on endpoint functionality would be more secure.

allObjections.title: §2: Redesign implementation scope
allObjections.detail: The 'redesign_implementation' class allows operator-declared scope, bounded by system caps. This introduces potential for operator error or malicious intent to declare a scope near the system cap, leading to unintended consequences or security vulnerabilities. The system cap itself might be too high.

allObjections.title: DLP pillar complexity
allObjections.detail: The 5th pillar in §3.3 introduces significant complexity, especially the requirement for a pre-migration backup and its verification. This could slow down the development process and introduce new failure points.

allObjections.title: Rate-limiting false positives
allObjections.detail: The 8th pillar in §3.4, which tests rate-limiting, might generate false positives if the endpoint is designed to handle bursts of traffic differently. This could lead to unnecessary rejections of valid constructions.

allObjections.title: SSRF probe limitations
allObjections.detail: The SSRF probes in §3.4 are limited to a predefined set of payloads. This might not cover all possible SSRF attack vectors, leaving the system vulnerable to more sophisticated attacks.

allObjections.title: Backup check is too late
allObjections.detail: In §3.3 S3 v2, the destructive migration can still be approved if the backup is merely taken and verified, but the test is framed after the operator has already authorized the statement. That means the system can spend time and operational risk preparing a destructive change before discovering the backup path is broken, which is the wrong failure point for a build/wire gate.

allObjections.title: Admin role is under-specified
allObjections.detail: The new DLP pillar says operator role must be `admin`, but it does not define how that role is asserted, audited, or prevented from being spoofed in the `governance_record_entry`. Because the proposal is explicitly about construction classes and PR gates, an ambiguous role check is a direct policy bypass surface rather than a protective control.

allObjections.title: TRUNCATE coverage is incomplete
allObjections.detail: §3.3 names `DROP COLUMN`, `DROP TABLE`, and `TRUNCATE`, but the phrase "any statement that destroys persistent rows" is broader than the explicit examples and can be interpreted inconsistently across SQL dialects and ORMs. That ambiguity invites accidental approval of destructive operations like `DELETE FROM` without a WHERE clause, partition drops, or cascading foreign-key effects that the text does not clearly bind.

allObjections.title: Authz snapshot can miss behavior
allObjections.detail: In §3.4 S4 v2, the extended authorization regression checks only snapshot `{endpoint_path, method, required_role[], auth_middleware_chain[]}`. That can miss effective permission changes caused by policy engines, route wrappers, middleware order changes, or context-sensitive checks that live outside those arrays, so the system may falsely certify a weakened endpoint as safe.

allObjections.title: SSRF probes are narrow
allObjections.detail: The new SSRF pillar enumerates a useful payload set, but it still treats detection as a small allowlist of probe classes rather than a general sink-to-egress analysis. A construction could pass the listed probes while still allowing redirects, non-HTTP schemes, DNS-based exfiltration, or indirect fetches through helper libraries.

allObjections.title: Overly Complex S3 Tests
allObjections.detail: The addition of a 5th pillar to S3 introduces significant complexity with the data-loss prevention checks, which may be prone to false positives or negatives.

allObjections.title: S4 Scope Creep
allObjections.detail: Extending S4 to 8 pillars with new tests like SSRF and rate-limit probing significantly broadens the security testing scope, potentially introducing new vulnerabilities or test fragility.

allObjections.title: Potential for Overly Restrictive Policies
allObjections.detail: The requirement for admin role and verified pg_dump backup for destructive migrations in S3 v2 may be overly restrictive and could hinder development or operational efficiency.

allObjections.title: S3 DLP lacks Self-Protect tie-in
allObjections.detail: §3.3 requires pg_dump backup + checksum for DROP operations but never references the §10 Self-Protect snapshot/rollback infrastructure; a failed post-backup migration can leave the live DB inconsistent with the governance_record_entry.

allObjections.title: S4 authz snapshot undefined for new endpoints
allObjections.detail: §3.4 pillar 6 mandates pre-construction authz snapshot for every touched endpoint yet provides no mechanism or storage format when the endpoint itself is created by an endpoint_generation class construction.

allObjections.title: Non-overridable conflicts with Locked Rule 13
allObjections.detail: §3.4 declares S4 NON-OVERRIDABLE per CEO Locked Rule 13, but canonical §25 rule 13 explicitly grants CEO absolute veto and Panel approval rights, creating an unresolvable precedence clash on any security-abort decision.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: If an operator approves a DROP COLUMN change and the backup verification is miswired or slow, the pipeline may proceed under a false sense of safety and only fail after partial destructive execution in downstream tooling. adversarial.precedent: GitHub Actions and other CI systems have repeatedly shown that broad trust in metadata-based role checks and artifact verification can be brittle; many supply-chain incidents exploited overly permissive workflow context or insufficiently verified artifacts. A closer precedent is database migration tooling in production systems where `DROP COLUMN` was allowed through automation and the backup/restore path turned out not to be restorable in practice, causing irreversible data loss.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: The strongest reason to reject or defer this proposal is that it converts high-blast-radius destructive database work and endpoint-security certification into always-on build/wire machinery before the verification model is mature. Even with the added pillars, the spec still leaves room for false confidence from partial snapshots and payload-based probing, and a mistaken pass would create a safer-looking but actually more dangerous deployment pipeline. Deferring until destructive migrations and security hardening are separated into more specialized, operator-heavy flows would reduce the chance of institutionalizing a flawed gate.

J2v2-S3.rationale: This keeps high-risk data destruction out of the build/wire path and preserves a clearer separation between wiring work and irreversible schema operations. The S3 DLP controls are useful, but they are not yet strong enough to justify merging destructive migrations into this engine.

J2v2-S4.pick_text: REJECT — none of the listed options is acceptable as specified
J2v2-S4.rationale: The proposal strengthens S4 in the right direction, but all listed options either under-scope the missing attack classes or overreach by bundling unrelated extras. A better answer would preserve the 8 pillars while also adding broader authz-context and SSRF/redirect coverage, which is not one of the available choices.

perReviewer.overallNotes: I am voting reject/defer on both questions because the drafted controls are directionally good but still leave important bypass and blast-radius gaps. The objections are about specification quality and failure containment, not about the value of the underlying safety goals.

J2v2-S4.rationale: CSRF protection is crucial for state-changing endpoints, and adding this check would further enhance the security posture of the build/wire engine.

perReviewer.overallNotes: The proposal introduces significant enhancements to security and data protection but also adds complexity and potential operational challenges.

objections.title: S3 DLP lacks Self-Protect tie-in
objections.detail: §3.3 requires pg_dump backup + checksum for DROP operations but never references the §10 Self-Protect snapshot/rollback infrastructure; a failed post-backup migration can leave the live DB inconsistent with the governance_record_entry.

objections.title: S4 authz snapshot undefined for new endpoints
objections.detail: §3.4 pillar 6 mandates pre-construction authz snapshot for every touched endpoint yet provides no mechanism or storage format when the endpoint itself is created by an endpoint_generation class construction.

objections.title: Non-overridable conflicts with Locked Rule 13
objections.detail: §3.4 declares S4 NON-OVERRIDABLE per CEO Locked Rule 13, but canonical §25 rule 13 explicitly grants CEO absolute veto and Panel approval rights, creating an unresolvable precedence clash on any security-abort decision.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: The eight-pillar S4 gate plus mandatory admin-only DLP checks will cause every non-trivial schema or endpoint change to abort on the first SSRF or rate-limit probe, freezing the wire-up pipeline and forcing manual workarounds that bypass all recorded governance entries.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: The proposal layers irreversible destructive-migration and security gates on top of an already complex Self-Governance Layer without defining how the new pillars interact with existing Human Gates or the 26-agent roster lock; deferral is warranted until those cross-references and failure-recovery paths are specified.

J2v2-S3.pick_text: REJECT — none of the listed options is acceptable as specified
J2v2-S3.rationale: None of the options address the missing integration between DLP and the §10 Self-Protect rollback path.

J2v2-S4.pick_text: REJECT — none of the listed options is acceptable as specified
J2v2-S4.rationale: All options assume the current 8-pillar design is coherent; the authz snapshot gap and Locked Rule 13 conflict make the whole suite unsound.
